Advaitācārya
------------------------------------------
At a time when the common masses of India were oppressed by the fanatical Muslim rulers on one side and the tyranny of the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् on the other, the भक्ति Movement (the Hindu spiritual renaissance through भक्ति or devotion to God) started and sustained by a galaxy of great spiritual leaders from Rāmānuja to चैतन्य (11th to 16th centuries A. D.) came as a great saviour. One of the important predecessors and a senior contemporary of चैतन्य was अद्वैताचार्य (16th Century A. D.) also known as Advaita or Advaita Prabhu. Not much is known of him. He was a resident of Śāntipur and a disciple of Mādhavendra पुरी. It was in his होउसे that चैतन्य met his मोथेर् शची देवी for the first time after taking to the monastic life, and decided to stay at पुरी (Orissa) for the rest of his life in deference to her wish.
Even before Viśvambhar—that is how चैतन्य was known in his premonastic days—was acclaimed as a great devotee of कृष्ण by the contemporary Vaiṣṇava leaders, अद्वैताचार्य had had visions of him as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of कृष्ण himself.
According to the theology developed by the later चैतन्य school, अद्वैताचार्य was an aspect of विष्णु.

Advaita-siddhi
(‘fulfilment of Advaita’)
------------------------------------------
If Hindu philosophical systems have grown both in width and depth revealing power and energy, it is not a little due to the freedom of thought enjoyed by the various writers. It was perhaps शङ्कर (A.

-820) the doyen of Advaita Vedānta who initiated and also gave a fillip to voluminous writing on abstruse philosophical subjects. Criticism, defence and counter-criticism of his views by sub-sequent writers gave rise to a phenomenal growth of Vedānta literature. When व्यास Tīrtha, a pontiff of the Mādhva school (15th-16th cent. A. D.) caused a jolt to Advaita metaphysics by his well-known polemical work Nyāyāmṛta, the Advaita tradition met his challenge through the Advaitasiddhi, the most celebrated work of मधुसूदन सरस्वती (16th cent. A. D.).
The point of dispute between the two works is the definition of what is true (satya) and what is false (mithyā). Any object is considered as सत्य (true, real) only as long as it is not बाधित (contradicted or negated) by subsequent experience. All the criticisms of Nyāyāmṛta against the five definitions of falsity given by the previous writers on Advaita have been met by the Advaitasiddhi. The book also discusses and supports many of the conflicting theories regarding the unity or plurality of the selves, unity or plurality of अविद्या (nescience), ब्रह्मन् or the जीव as the locus of अविद्या thereby implying that any of the theories can be resorted to in explaining the indeterminable false world since the main interest of the advaitin is the one absolute ब्रह्मन्. The different theories of Advaita can be adopted by the different aspirants according to their fitness (adhikāra).
The work has three Sanskrit commen-taries of which Laghucandrikā of ब्रह्मा-नन्द सरस्वती is popular among the scholars.
See also ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA, MADHUSŪDANA SARASVATĪ, NYĀYĀMṚTA and VYĀSATĪRTHA.

Advayatāraka Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
It is a minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda and classed among the ‘Yoga-उपनिषद्स्,’ उपनिषद्स् that deal with yogic meditations and other processes. Except for the last part which is in verses (14 to 18), the whole Upaniṣad is in elegant prose.
It has been called ‘Advayatāraka’ since it deals with ब्रह्मन्, the one without a second (‘advaya’), which takes us beyond (‘tāraka’) सṁसार or transmigratory existence.
The Upaniṣad begins with the statement that it has to be taught to one who is struggling to meditate upon ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, (‘yati,’ ‘one who struggles’) who has practised self-control (‘jitendriya’) and who has cultivated the six virtues like peace (‘śamādiṣaṭka’). Then it describes that one who meditates upon light in between the eyebrows as ब्रह्मन् attains to It. After negating the difference between the jīvātman (individual self) and ईश्वर (Supreme सोउल्) as brought about by the limiting adjuncts like māyā, it goes on to describe a yogic meditation for attaining ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
The सुषुम्ना-nāḍī (a tube-like structure meant for the passage of the कुण्डलिनी) (See KUṆḌALINĪ.) is situated in the middle of the body, stretching from the mulādhāra plexus at the root of the spinal column, up to the ब्रह्मरन्ध्र or the aperture in the crown of the head. It shines like the sun or the मोओन्. The कुण्डलिनी which is fine like the thread in the lotus stalk, is inside this सुषुम्ना and is shining like millions of lightnings. By closing the ears and meditating on the sound within and the blue light within, between the eyes, and witnessing it, one gets infinite happiness. This is meditation on the ‘inside.’
The Upaniṣad then proceeds to describe the process of meditation on two points, ‘outside’ and ‘in between’ the ‘inside’ and the ‘outside.’ The first consists in fixing the gaze and the मिन्द् at any point in front of the nose, 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12 aṅgulas (an अङ्गुल is roughly about an inch) in distance, seeing it as of blue-yellow colour. The latter consists of meditating on the ‘ākāśa’ or ether/space, near the tip of the nose but beyond it, and as being bright like the full sun of the morning or fire with leaping tongues. In both cases this light becomes a symbol for ब्रह्मन्.
Then comes the description of ‘tārakayoga,’ meditation on the light in the head, by reversing the mental light into the area between the eye brows, inside the head but towards the crown. Such meditation can give the supernatural ‘aṣṭasiddhis’ or ‘eight powers.’
Last comes the शाम्भवीमुद्रा. It is the same as meditation already described, but, with the eyes without being closed or opened.
The Upaniṣad ends with a description of the qualifications of the गुरु fit to teach such योग.
See also ŚĀMBHAVĪMUDRĀ and UPA-NIṢADS.

Advaita Vedānta Darśana
(‘Non-dual Vedānta System’)
------------------------------------------
PREAMBLE
Man is often described as a rational animal. Once the animal in him is reasonably satisfied by the provision of basic biological and some psychological needs, the rational part gets an opportunity to evolve to higher levels. Philosophy including metaphysics is one of the highest aspects of this evolution.
DARŚANAS
The Indian philosophical systems have developed not only as a result of intellectual speculation but also of mystical intuition. Hence the name ‘darśana’ (lit., ‘seeing’), usually applied to them. The topics most commonly discussed by these darśanas are generally four:
nature of the physical world, its origin and evolution;
nature of man and other living beings;
existence of God, his nature and attributes;
the goal of human life and the way of attaining it.
Different standpoints and differing views of these topics of discussion have naturally led to a variety of schools. These schools are broadly divided into two classes: the आस्तिक and the नास्तिक. The former accept the authority of the वेदस् whereas the latter do not.
VEDĀNTA DARŚANA
The वेदान्त दर्शन is the last of the former schools but has gained the most important place among them. A judicious combination of reasoning and acceptance of the authority of the वेदस् as also a long unbroken tradition are responsible for its gaining the pre-eminent place.
Though the ‘prasthānatraya’ (‘the three great paths’) viz., the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā, are the basis of the वेदान्त दर्शन, it is the Brahmasūtras (also called Vedānta-sūtras and Śārīrakasūtras) of बादरायण-व्यास that occupies the key position. The sūtras (aphorisms) being quite terse and often ambiguous have naturally led to widely differing interpretations, resulting in the three well-known systems of Vedānta viz., Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत.
The word ‘Vedānta’ itself means the ‘end or the essence of the वेदस्.’ It is the उपनिषद्स् that mainly comprise the Vedānta since they normally form the last part of the Vedic literature and contain the quintessence of their teachings.
ADVAITA VEDĀNTA
The अद्वैत वेदान्त दर्शन owes its systematisation as a formidable doctrine, to गौडपाद (7th-8th cent. A.D.) who wrote his famous Kārikās on the Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad and शङ्कर (A.

-820). शङ्कर’s commentaries on the प्रस्थानत्रय as also a few independent treatises form the bedrock on which the later Advaitins built their edifices.
‘Advaita’ means ‘non-dual’, ‘one without a second’. The system derives this nomenclature from the fact that it recognises ब्रह्मन् (the Absolute) as the only reality and denies permanent reality to the world as also to the individual souls.
The entire edifice of Advaita metaphysics is built upon the foundation that ब्रह्मन् is the only reality, ‘brahma satyam’. This premise is based firmly on the famous Upaniṣadic statement ‘sadeva somya idamagra āsīt, ekamevādvitīyam.’ ‘Dear (Śvetaketu), in the beginning (before च्रेअतिओन्) Reality (or ब्रह्मन्) alone existed, the one without a second’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad

). However, the world of multiplicity is a matter of our day-to-day experience. Hence it becomes necessary to offer an explanation as to how ब्रह्मन्, the one without a second, appears as this world of multiple names and forms. The explanation offered by Advaita is ‘Anirvacanīyakhyāti,’ its theory of erroneous चोग्नितिओन्, which defies लोगिच्. (For other theories about erroneous चोग्नितिओन् see KHYĀTIS.) Perceiving silver in nacre in moonlight or snake in rope in insufficient light are stock examples given by the Advaitins. In both cases there is an erroneous perception brought about by the impressions of silver and snake from an earlier idea of the same, now superimposed upon nacre and rope under conditions favourable to the error. This superimposition called ‘adhyāsa’ or ‘adhyāropa’, is responsible for the mithyājñāna (false knowledge) that the object perceived is silver or snake.
The silver or the snake perceived is neither ‘sat’ (real) nor ‘asat’ (unreal). It is not असत् or unreal like ‘the son of a barren woman’ since it is actually perceived. Neither is it sat or real since it disappears as soon as the substratum (the nacre and the rope) is perceived as it is. To explain such a peculiar phenomenon शङ्कर creates, out of logical necessity, a third type of perceived objects which is ‘sad-asad-vilakṣaṇa’ (different from both the real and the unreal). The ‘khyāti’ or the चोग्नितिओन् itself is described as ‘anirvacanīya,’ incapable of any precise definition or description.
The basic cause of this erroneous perception is termed ‘ajñāna’ or ‘avidyā’ (ignorance) which is said to be भावरूप (existent) and is endowed with two śaktis or powers viz., ‘āvaraṇaśakti’ (veiling power) and ‘vikṣepaśakti’ (transforming power). It veils the true nature of nacre and rope and shows up silver and snake in their place by apparently transforming them. Such an apparently transformed object is called a ‘vivarta’ of the original and the theory that propounds this is known as ‘Vivartavāda.’
Since this अविद्या does not make the nacre and the rope completely disappear from view, but only makes them appear as something else, it is described as भावरूप or existent.
An attempt may now be made to explain how this world of duality has evolved out of the non-dual Reality called ब्रह्मन् in the उपनिषद्स्. The world of duality can be broadly divided into ‘dṛk’ (the seer) and ‘dṛśya’ (the seen). Both these again are divided into the innumerable living beings (jīvās) and the countless objects of च्रेअतिओन्. How does ब्रह्मन् the Absolute, the One without a second, the indivisible Reality, appear divided into innumerable beings on the one side and countless objects on the other? It is अविद्या that causes the one आत्मन् (the Self)—incidentally, the उपनिषद्स् use both words, आत्मन् and ब्रह्मन्, to indicate the same Reality—appear as many jīvas and it is māyā that causes the world of phenomena. Māyā is अविद्या at the cosmic level.
Śaṅkara accepts three degrees of reality. The first, known as ‘prātibhāsika-सत्य’ (apparent truth, illusory appearance) is illustrated in the wrong perception of silver in nacre or snake in rope. The second, called ‘vyāvahārika-सत्य’ is illustrated by this world of our day-to-day experience. This world-appearance has a much higher degree of reality and lasts till one gets आत्मज्ञान or ब्रह्मज्ञान, realization of the Truth, आत्मन्-ब्रह्मन्. It is सत्य or true for all purposes of vyavahāra i.e., day-to-day existence or practical life. The third, designated as ‘pāramārthika-सत्य,’ is the highest Truth and the only truth that really exists. It is ब्रह्मन् or आत्मन्, which is nirguṇa (without attributes) and nirākāra (without forms), hence incapable of being described except in a negative way (‘neti,’ ‘neti’—‘not this, not this’).
Brahman associated with māyā is Saguṇa ब्रह्मन् (Brahman with attri-butes) or ईश्वर (Lord of च्रेअतिओन्, God). It is this aspect of ब्रह्मन् that is responsible for च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction of the world. As for the actual order of evolution of the created world, the descriptions given in the उपनिषद्स् are accepted.
For शङ्कर who holds that the world process is only a ‘vivarta’ (illusory appearance) due to अध्यास (superimposition) on ब्रह्मन्, the very attempt to describe the various steps of evolution is a futile exercise. However, since the śruti (revealed scripture, the उपनिषद्स्) has done so, a place of honour must somehow be accorded to it. Hence he characterises such descriptions as giving the ‘taṭastha-lakṣaṇa’ (accidental or casual charac-teristics) of ब्रह्मन् helping us to be directed towards it, even as the branch of a tree helps us to locate the crescent in the sky. On the other hand ब्रह्मन् as it is, can be comprehended only through its ‘svarūpalakṣaṇa’ (integral or essential characteristics), which is ‘sat-cit-आनन्द.’ ‘Sat’ (eternal reality), ‘cit’ (pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्), and ‘ānanda’ (unalloyed bliss) are not really its characteristics but its very essence.
This ब्रह्मन् or आत्मन् which is sat-cit-आनन्द, has inexplicably got itself involved in the body-मिन्द् complex, the involvement being due to अविद्या. Since the origin of this involvement can never be logically or satisfactorily explained, अविद्या is stated to be anādi or beginningless. The involved आत्मन् is designated as ‘jīva.’
This जीव, the आत्मन् in bondage, has five kośas or sheaths (For details see PAÑCAKOŚAS.), three śarīras or bodies (See STHŪLAŚARĪRA, SŪKṢMAŚARĪRA and KĀRAṆA-ŚARĪRA.), performs actions motivated by desires, experiences pleasure and pain due to कर्म and undergoes transmigration (See KARMA and PUNARJANMA.) until libera-tion. शङ्कर declares that this जीव, when shorn of its upādhis or limiting adjuncts like the body and the मिन्द्, is identical with ब्रह्मन्, since its essential nature also is sat-cit-आनन्द.
The main trouble with the आत्मन् become जीव is the tādātmya or false identification with the मिन्द् and the body brought about by अध्यारोप or अध्यास (superimposition). Hence the only way of remedying it is by अपवाद or desuper-imposition, denying this identification. For this, one has first to prepare oneself by the preliminary fourfold discipline or sādhana-catuṣṭaya viz., विवेक (discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal), वैराग्य (dispassion), śamādi-ṣaṭka (cultivation of the six virtues like self-control) and मुमुक्षुत्व (desire for लिबेरतिओन्). (For details see SĀDHANA-CATUṢṬAYA.) Then one has to approach a competent गुरु (spiritual preceptor) and learn the truth from him by śravaṇa (hearing), मनन (reflection) and nidi-dhyāsana (contemplation). The most important part of the गुरु’s teaching will be in the form of ‘mahāvākyas’ (great sentences) like ‘tat tvam asi’ (That thou art’) or ‘ahaṁ brahmāsmi’ (‘I am ब्रह्मन्’). (See MAHĀVĀKYAS for details.) Śravaṇa and मनन produce the deep-rooted conviction that one is the spirit. Hence in निदिध्यासन, desuperimposition in the form of ‘I am not the body, nor the sense-organs, nor the मिन्द्, nor even the ego’ and so on, can be practised leading ultimately to the realization that one is the आत्मन्. This realization resulting in मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् can be had even while one is living in this body. It is known as ‘jīvanmukti.’ He will attain ‘videhamukti’ after the body falls off, the continuance of the body between the two states being due to prārabdha-कर्म. (See PRĀRABDHA KARMA.)
Mukti or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigration is not the gaining of a new state but recognising the already existing original state.
Two kinds of mukti—jīvanmukti and videhamukti—are envisaged in the Advaitic works. The Vivaraṇa school upholds the theory that मुक्ति is simultaneous with ज्ञान. Hence जीवन्मुक्ति is not only possible, but the only मुक्ति that can be recognised. Continuance of the body for some more time, due to prārabdha कर्म, has no effect upon ज्ञान. On the other hand, the भामती school holds that even after ज्ञान, if the body continues due to prārabdha कर्म, this imposes a limitation thereby implying the existence of a trace of अविद्या. The death of the body puts an end even to this trace of अविद्या, and real मुक्ति is obtained then. Since this comes after the death of the body, it is called ‘videhamukti.’
A favourite topic of discussion that frequently crops up in Advaita metaphysical works is the locus of अविद्या. Since ब्रह्मन् is the only reality that exists, it alone is the āśraya (locus) as also the viṣaya (object) of अविद्या. This is one school. सुरेश्वर and पद्मपाद are the main protagonists of this school. According to them अविद्या is one only.
Since ब्रह्मन् is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, अविद्या can never exist in it nor act on it. This is the opposing school propagated by वाचस्पति मिश्र. For him, the jīvas are the loci of अविद्या and there is one अविद्या for every जीव.
POST-शङ्कर ADVAITA
Though शङ्कर wrote profusely, clearly enunciating the main doctrines of his school, there are certain places in his writings wherein the important aspects of certain doctrines are either vague or are capable of more than one interpretation. This has naturally, resulted in the growth of quite a voluminous post-शङ्कर Advaita literature leading to different prasthānas or schools of thought. The ‘Vārttika-prasthāna’ of सुरेश्वर (9th cent. A. D.) comes first in the series. This school gets its designation from the exposition contained in the ‘vārttikās’ or commentaries in verse of सुरेश्वर on शङ्कर’s bhāṣyas on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Taittirīya उपनिषद्स्. According to this school, ब्रह्मन् is the material cause of this world, and not māyā. The locus of अविद्या is ब्रह्मन् and not the jīvas. अविद्या is one only and not many. The महावाक्यस् or the great Vedic dictums are capable of producing immediate चोग्नितिओन् of the Self as ब्रह्मन्. Hence dhyānābhyāsa or practice of meditation on the meaning of those dictums is not necessary. The jīvas are but ābhāsas or appearances of ब्रह्मन् in the individual minds. (This has earned the theory, the designation of ‘ābhāsavāda’ as opposed to ‘pratibimbavāda’ and ‘avaccheda-वाद’ of other schools.)
The ‘Vivaraṇaprasthāna’ of पद्म-pāda (9th cent. A. D.) and प्रकाशात्मन् (A.

) comes next. The name is derived from the work Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa of the latter, it being a voluminous commentary on the Pañcapādikā of पद्मपाद, which itself is a commentary on Śaṇkara’s ब्रह्मसूत्र-bhāsya. Though this name suggests that it covers five pādas or sections of the Brahmasūtras, only the commentary on the first four sūtras is now available. The chief doctrines of this school are: अविद्या is a jaḍātmikā शक्ति (a force of material nature) and is the material cause of this world. It is भावरूप, a positive entity but not real. Māyā, प्रकृति, अव्यक्त, avyākṛta, तमस्, शक्ति etc., are all its synonyms. It is called अविद्या when आवरण power is predominant and māyā when विक्षेप power becomes dominant. Alternatively, it is māyā at the cosmic level and अविद्या at the individual level. अविद्या rests on ब्रह्मन् but acts on the jīvas. The jīvās are pratibimbas or reflections of ब्रह्मन् in the अन्तःकरण (mind). The reflected images have no reality other than that of the original (bimba) ब्रह्मन्. This theory is called ‘pratibimbavāda’ and contrasted with ‘ābhāsavāda’.
The ‘Bhāmatīprasthāna’ of वाचस्पति मिश्र (A.

) is the third and the last of these major schools. Bhāmatī is his celebrated commentary on the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya of Brahmasūtras. This school is built round the Bhāmatī along with its subsidiary commentaries Kalpataru of Amalānanda (13th cent A. D.). and Parimalā of अप्पय्य दीक्षित (16th cent A. D.) The views of this school can be briefly summarised as follows: ब्रह्मन् is the material cause of the world, not as the locus of अविद्या but as the object of avidyās supported by the jīvas. Māyā is only an accessory cause. अविद्या cannot abide in ब्रह्मन्. It abides in the jīvas and is plural since the jīvas are plural. वाचस्पति advocates two varieties of अविद्या: the मूलाविद्या or kāraṇāvidyā (primal nescience); the tūlāvidyā or kāryāvidyā (derivative nescience). It is the latter that is responsible for भ्रम-सṁस्कारस् or error impressions. Also, वाचस्पति appears more inclined towards the ‘avacchedavāda’ or the theory of limitation with regard to the appearance of the jīvas. Just as a pot limits the infinite sky in itself, अविद्या of the individual limits ब्रह्मन् and makes it appear like a जीव. Another point of importance in this school is that the महावाक्यस् do not produce anubhava (immediate चोग्नितिओन्). It is the मिन्द् seasoned by meditation that gives such experience.
Mention may also be made here of ‘dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi-वाद’ which advocates that the world is created simultaneously with its perceptions, and, ‘ekajīvavāda,’ which propounds that there is only one जीव which is in bondage and when it gets लिबेरतिओन्, everything else disappears. Prakāśānanda (15th-16th cent. A. D.) is the chief exponent of these schools.
Advaita was subjected to continuous criticism by other Vedāntic schools as also the Buddhists and hence the growth of polemical literature became inevitable. Mention must be made of two most important works of this type: The Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍa-khādya of श्रीहर्ष (12th cent. A.D.) and the Advaitasiddhi of मधुसूदन सरस्वती (16th cent. A. D.).
CONCLUSION
It should be said to the credit of Advaita Vedānta that even now it is attracting the respectful attention from scholars of the highest calibre, both Eastern and Western.
NOTE :
The number of connected topics is too large to be mentioned separately for cross reference. The reader can look for them under the respective titles as he comes across them in this essay.
